title: China's stock market sinks into bear territory as CSI 300 extends 10-week rout
description: General view of tourists taking selfies at North Bund in Shanghai, China, as Typhoon Dolphin approaches the country.Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty Images
body: General view of tourists taking selfies at North Bund in Shanghai, China, as Typhoon Dolphin approaches the country.Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesChina's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment."I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC."For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities."It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

schema.headline: China's stock market sinks into bear territory as CSI 300 extends 10-week rout

title: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms
description: An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Sept. 19, 2026.AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. ordered non-emergency
body: An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Sept. 19, 2026.AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate.The move comes as the U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, according to The New York Times, citing unnamed U.S. officials. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.  The developments point to a possible widening of the nearly eight-month war, while U.S. and Iranian negotiators continue talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets. Meanwhile, Reuters reported Washington also plans to withdraw family members from other missions in the region.A strike Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least one person and injured eight. Two people died in a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field, the Saudi Press Agency reported, adding that operations were not affected.In recent days, the U.S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up military exercises, including flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers, according to The New York Times. The Times also reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel this week to discuss potential new strikes. The renewed military strikes would likely target Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal, according to The Times, noting that President Donald Trump has yet to approve the fresh strikes and has repeatedly vetoed plans for a return to major combat this year. Iranian officials have vowed to widen their attacks to target data centers and undersea internet cables, while refusing concessions on their nuclear program. Despite the persistent shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Middle East oil flows through the vital strait have recovered to near pre‑war levels according to Kpler. As Brent crude topped $110 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate gained 1% to $98.12, recovering appetite for crude from China could drive oil prices higher, according to the commodity research firm.   "China's crude import demand is expected to continue recovering, driven by rising refinery throughput and rapidly declining crude inventories," said Muyu Xu, senior crude oil analyst at Kpler. The war has cut China's oil stockpiles, with the fastest drawndown on record at 1.6 million barrels a day in September, Xu estimated.China still holds 1.1 billion barrels in reserves, about 80 days of refinery needs, Xu said. She added that with virtually all Iranian cargoes outside the U.S. blockade discharged, substantial new crude arrivals in China appear unlikely.Chinese state-owned refiners are likely to have a stronger appetite and greater urgency to secure prompt Middle Eastern barrels as they face higher throughput and inventory-replenishment needs. Independent refiners are also seeking alternatives to Iranian crude, a shift that could limit further downside in the Dubai structure, Xu said.

schema.headline: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms

title: Barclays to slash 5,000 jobs in AI efficiency push
description: British lender Barclays has revealed plans to cut 5,000 jobs — about 5% of its total workforce — as part of an artificial intelligence-linked efficien
body: British lender Barclays has revealed plans to cut 5,000 jobs — about 5% of its total workforce — as part of an artificial intelligence-linked efficiency push.In its third-quarter earnings statement Thursday, Barclays said it was "structurally reducing the cost base to generate capacity for investment."About 60% of the cuts are expected to be in support functions, including developers, according to the earnings presentation, which also noted an outcome was "organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI."watch nowShares in the bank were almost 1% lower by 8:50 a.m. in London (3:50 a.m. E.T.), less than an hour into the trading day.Barclays' third-quarter pre-tax profit rose 12% year on year to £2.3 billion ($3.1 billion), matching LSEG-compiled forecasts. Group income for the period was £7.4 billion, below analysts' estimate of £7.61 billion.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBarclays.Net interest income was broadly unchanged at £3.91 billion. Its CET1 capital ratio, a measure of financial solvency, edged down to 14.2% from 14.3% at the end of the second quarter. Return on tangible equity fell to 11.7% from 16.1%.

schema.headline: Barclays to slash 5,000 jobs in AI efficiency push

title: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond
description: 21 October 2026, Baden-Württemberg, Stuttgart: When visiting the website of the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of the Interior, a warning message appears
body: 21 October 2026, Baden-Württemberg, Stuttgart: When visiting the website of the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of the Interior, a warning message appears in the browser indicating a potential security issue. A serious security vulnerability is threatening websites worldwide; blogs, online stores, and news portals could become targets for attackers. The PHP vulnerability allows attackers to take over entire servers. Photo: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa (Photo by Bernd Weißbrod/picture alliance via Getty Images)Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesThe tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet.The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems.The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks.The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible.The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk.Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems. Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure.Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches.OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure.The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals.Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates.The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses.

schema.headline: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond

title: Southwest Airlines cuts 2026 profit forecast on higher fuel
description: A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 airplane departs from San Diego International Airport on May 27, 2026.Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesS
body: A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 airplane departs from San Diego International Airport on May 27, 2026.Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesSouthwest Airlines became the third major U.S. airline this month to cut its 2026 profit forecast due to higher fuel prices, but CEO Bob Jordan said travelers continue to book despite higher fares.The carrier expects to earn between $2.60 and $2.85 a share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its forecast in July of between $3.25 to as much as $4.25 a share.Here's what Southwest reported for third quarter compared with Wall Street expectations, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:Earnings per share: 66 cents adjusted vs. 58 cents expectedRevenue: $8.42 billion adjusted vs. $8.25 billion expectedSouthwest forecast per-share adjusted earnings of between 55 cents and 80 cents in the fourth quarter and unit revenue, a gauge of airfare, up as much as 21% from a year earlier. It said it expects to grow capacity by up to 4% year over year."Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," Jordan said in an earnings release.The airline said its average passenger fare was $231.69 in the third quarter, up almost 27% from the same quarter of 2025. A spokesman said that number does not include add-on fees. The number of revenue passengers carried fell 3.2% to 33.47 million people.Under pressure to grow revenue, Southwest has been remaking its longtime business model over the past several years, scrapping its old policies like two free checked bags per passenger and open seating. In its place, Southwest has started charging for many seat assignments and added a bag fee, similar to major competitors.For the third quarter, Southwest posted net income of $270 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $54 million or 10 cents a share a year earlier. Revenue rose more than 21% to $8.42 billion.Adjusting for one-time items, Southwest reported 66 cents a share.Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also cut their profit outlooks for the rest of the year when they reported third-quarter earnings. Both of those airlines reported top- and bottom-line misses for the third quarter.Read more CNBC airline newsWhy airfare could rise even more, but airline profits won’tBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to premium upgradesCompanies spurn airlines’ cheapest business class ticketsUnited’s next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years agoRecord heat, crowds drive offseason boom in international travel

title: Sovereign wealth funds' China and Hong Kong investments surge 190% after a bruising slump
description: LANZHOU, CHINA - SEPTEMBER 29: Flowers and Chinese national flags decorate the Jinyan Yellow River Bridge on September 29, 2026 in Lanzhou, Gansu Prov
body: LANZHOU, CHINA - SEPTEMBER 29: Flowers and Chinese national flags decorate the Jinyan Yellow River Bridge on September 29, 2026 in Lanzhou, Gansu Province of China. China News Service | Getty ImagesSovereign wealth funds are pouring billions of dollars back into mainland China and Hong Kong, reversing a sharp investment slump, with Middle Eastern investors leading the charge. Investments into mainland China and Hong Kong surged to $14.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, surging 190% compared with the funds' investments through the entire 2025, according to data provided to CNBC by Singapore-based consultancy Global SWF. That's in stark contrast to a 54% plunge in 2025 from the prior year as geopolitical tensions and concerns over China's economic outlook weighed on investor sentiment.The resurgence this year has been driven largely by Middle Eastern sovereign investors, with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund alone accounting for $6 billion of the inflows, followed by Abu Dhabi Investment Authority's $2.5 billion, data from Global SWF showed. Abu Dhabi's Mubadala and Qatar Investment Authority have invested $800 million and $600 million, respectively.Together, the four Gulf funds accounted for nearly 70% of sovereign investments into China and Hong Kong during the period, underscoring the growing role of Middle Eastern capital in the region.Renewed interest in China comes as sovereign investors increasingly look beyond geopolitical tensions to capitalize on opportunities in Chinese technology, biotechnology, consumer businesses and advanced manufacturing."I think China has gone from 'China is not investable’ to ‘is China investable?’ to today, the most common question I get is: ‘are we missing out?'" said Jenny Lee, senior managing partner at investment management firm Granite Asia.Lee said China's established strengths in manufacturing and biotechnology could give it an advantage as AI development increasingly expands beyond frontier models into industry-specific applications, including robotics and drug discovery.China's extensive network of factories and research laboratories provides access to real-world data that could become increasingly valuable in developing these applications, she added.Drawing interestFor Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala, Asia in general has become an increasingly important destination as the sovereign investor seeks to diversify its portfolio and deepen exposure to long-term growth opportunities.Andrew Wang, who leads consumer division for private equity at Mubadala, said the firm sees compelling opportunities in China, citing attractive valuations and the country's vast consumer market as the fund continues to expand its presence in Asia."Valuations are lower than they've been in years. I think this will be a really good vintage for investors in China," Wang told CNBC. He said China was the fund's top priority for consumer investments in Asia, pointing to the potential for household consumption to expand and the growing competitiveness of Chinese brands.Chinese companies were increasingly moving beyond their reputation for producing inexpensive goods toward higher-value products, Wang said, as homegrown brands demonstrate stronger innovation and competitiveness globally. Mubadala announced a minority investment in China's Luckin Coffee in September, as part of a roughly $1 billion deal alongside Centurium Capital.From caution to conviction?Other big funds have also shown interest this year.Qatar Investment Authority and Norway's sovereign wealth fund participated in Alibaba's $10.2 billion share offering in August, while Singapore's Temasek is identifying opportunities in China, particularly in biotechnology, domestic consumer brands and AI-related hardware."China continues to be interesting," said Rohit Sipahimalani, Temasek's chief investment officer, at the Milken Summit in Singapore recently."Biotech in particular [is] a very exciting area out there which we're investing in. Local consumer brands could really be important," he said.Sipahimalani also pointed to China's growing competitiveness across the AI hardware supply chain, predicting that Chinese manufacturers could increasingly challenge established global players.Temasek was among the cornerstone investors in optical-components manufacturer Zhongji Innolight's multibillion-dollar initial public offering in July.Pandu Sjahrir, chief investment officer at Indonesian sovereign wealth fund Danantara, told CNBC that the fund was also looking to expand its cooperation with China beyond its existing partnerships in nickel processing and battery manufacturing, with growing interest in artificial intelligence, robotics, healthcare and energy efficiency. The Indonesian sovereign investor sees opportunities to build on its energy resources to develop AI-related digital infrastructure and downstream industries. “We now already have someone to head North Asia for us. She's also based in China, and her job as a team is "how do we develop long-term partnership, especially in the downstream side?" he said.Despite the sharp rebound, China remains a relatively small destination for sovereign wealth fund capital compared with Western markets.The U.S. attracted $132.4 billion in sovereign investments in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $44.6 billion for Europe and the U.K., according to Global SWF data. China and Hong Kong's $14.2 billion represented just a fraction of those flows.

schema.headline: Sovereign wealth funds' China and Hong Kong investments surge 190% after a bruising slump

title: Bank of Korea holds rates after President Lee calls for boosting housing supply
description: Shin Hyun Song, governor of the Bank of Korea, during a fireside chat at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangk
body: Shin Hyun Song, governor of the Bank of Korea, during a fireside chat at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.  Sirachai Arunrugstichai | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSouth Korea's central bank expectedly kept its policy rate steady at 3% on Thursday, after two straight hikes, with analysts pointing that it does not signal a change in policy stance as inflation stays elevated.Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the Bank of Korea to hold rates, and the decision comes after President Lee Jae Myung reportedly called for an "all out effort" to boost housing supply. The BOK in its statement said it opted to hold rates as it assesses the effects of the two prior rate hikes, and looks at "developments in both domestic and external risk factors," citing increasing uncertainties around the Middle East conflict and monetary and fiscal policies of major economies.Last week, BOK Governor Shin Hyun Song said at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings that the central bank will keep monetary policy restrictive until it's confident that inflation was heading back to target. "Inflation has really picked up, both from the cost-push and the demand-pull," Shin said. Inflation in Asia's fourth-largest economy came in at 2.9% in September, staying at or above the BOK's 2% target for 13 months. As President Lee pushes for increasing the housing supply, the BOK on Thursday flagged that "housing-related loans continued to increase and the pace of increase in housing prices in Seoul and its surrounding areas accelerated again."The Kospi was trading 1.23% lower, while the won strengthened marginally against the dollar to trade at 1,326.1. Given a strong economy and persistent inflation, a pause does not mean the end of the tightening cycle, according to Gareth Leather, senior Asia economist at Capital Economics. Leather foresees one more hike at BOK's meeting next month. South Korea's growth has been largely supported by exports of semiconductors as demand for chips to power the AI boom continues. Exports in September skyrocketed at a record 83.7% year on year, with semiconductor shipments surging 263% compared to the same period last year.The IMF has projected the country's growth at 3.3% for the whole of 2026. GDP growth for the country came in at 3.8% and 3.7% for the first and second quarters respectively, both times beating expectations. — CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Bank of Korea holds rates after President Lee calls for boosting housing supply

title: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion loss after bond market turbulence
description: Nicolai Tangen, chief executive officer of NBIM, at the Norges Bank Climate Conference in Oslo, Norway, on Oct. 21, 2025.Naina Helén Jåma | Bloomberg
body: Nicolai Tangen, chief executive officer of NBIM, at the Norges Bank Climate Conference in Oslo, Norway, on Oct. 21, 2025.Naina Helén Jåma | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNorway's sovereign wealth fund — the largest in the world — said Thursday that its investment portfolio delivered a loss of $30 billion in the third quarter, as rising interest rates dented returns on its bond holdings. Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages the $2.3 trillion fund, said the accounting return for the period was a loss of 278 billion kroner ($29.7 billion). Around 70% of NBIM's fixed income portfolio is allocated to government bonds, with the remainder invested in corporate debt.The third quarter saw a global bond market rout. Government bond yields surged as major central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve, began rate-hiking cycles and concerns about inflation and government debt levels mounted. NBIM's fixed income investments delivered a negative return of 3.5%, with the fund's management saying this was a key driver of the overall downturn. "The fund's return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments," NBIM's Deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement. Fixed income accounts for just over a quarter of the fund's entire portfolio, with NBIM invested in 1,664 bonds across 51 countries.Last month, NBIM said it wanted to cut its U.S. Treasury holdings as part of wider plans to reduce its allocation to government-issued debt.Equities, which account for 72% of the sovereign wealth fund's investments, returned 0.5% for the fund in the third quarter. The fund has small stakes in around 7,100 companies across most countries. With holdings in 1.5% of all listed companies globally, it is the world's largest single investor. Stock markets were turbulent in the three months to September. Wall Street's major averages ended the third quarter in mixed territory. The S&P 500 index added 2.03%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended the quarter 2.2% higher.The average change across the three indexes was just 0.6%, marking a slowdown in the rally that saw double-digit gains in the previous quarter.NBIM is an investor in America's biggest companies, with its top holdings including a $65.4 billion stake in Nvidia, as well as positions in Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft. Its positions in the world's biggest companies make NBIM influential in terms of both voting power and setting investment trends. "Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell," Grande said Thursday. Energy stocks benefited from surging oil prices in the third quarter, as the U.S.-Iran war continued, said NBIM, which has stakes in various energy majors, including Exxon Mobil, Shell and Chevron. Over the summer, NBIM CEO Nicolai Tangen told CNBC that investors should not expect a continuation of the bumper gains seen in the stock market in the first half of this year."For sure, we should not be expecting the same kind of returns going forward as we've seen over the last six months," he said at the time. The fund delivered a first-half return of 12.95%, and a record first-half profit nearing $185 billion. It also invests in real estate and renewable energy infrastructure, which returned 0.4% and 7.5%, respectively, in the third quarter. Norway established its sovereign wealth fund in 1998 to invest revenues from the country's oil.

schema.headline: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion loss after bond market turbulence

title: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds
description: Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026.Aaron Clamage | CNBCInvestors may be wary of the volatility hi
body: Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026.Aaron Clamage | CNBCInvestors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration."Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday. That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus. The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconiShares Flexible Income Active ETF year to dateBest opportunities include hyperscalersRieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3. That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG. "They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it." Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%. That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised."Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names. "There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits. CoreWeave's 2031 bond yield on Oct. 21, 2026Fed watchRieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool. The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said."They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added. Calculating risks aheadRieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026."The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched. "With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

schema.headline: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

title: Netflix has dipped its toe into theatrical. Is it ready to jump in?
description: The Netflix logo is seen at the Egyptian Theatre ahead of the premiere for Netflix's "Running Point," Season 2, in Hollywood on April 15, 2026. Patric
body: The Netflix logo is seen at the Egyptian Theatre ahead of the premiere for Netflix's "Running Point," Season 2, in Hollywood on April 15, 2026. Patrick T. Fallon | Afp | Getty ImagesNetflix is making itself clear: It's a streaming-first business.During the company's third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday, co-CEO Ted Sarandos reiterated the streaming giant's long-held stance that its content, which it spent $20 billion on last year, is meant for its subscribers and, therefore, should be delivered to customers on its streaming platform as quickly as possible.Yet, the company is set to have 30 theatrical releases in 2027, on par with what it brought to cinemas in 2026. And while not all of these features are expected to have wide releases or long runs in theaters, Netflix is testing the waters with projects like Greta Gerwig's "Narnia: The Magician's Nephew," which will have a wide release and a 49-day exclusive theatrical window when it hits cinemas in February.The company seems poised to carve a new path forward as it grapples with viewership stagnation and a stock slump of roughly 30% since January. How its theatrical ambitions fit into a streaming-first strategy remains a question mark. "Theatrical releases are a net positive for reach and streaming demand," Alicia Reese, analyst at Wedbush, wrote in a note Wednesday. "Netflix's more amenable attitude toward exclusive theatrical windows will not only facilitate better relationships with talent, but also add a new revenue stream and build interest in its streaming service. This follows the pattern we have seen with the major studios' streaming platforms over the past several years: theatrical releases don't cannibalize the streaming window, as Netflix fears."Ahead of its Tuesday earnings report, Netflix restructured its C-suite, bringing in former Disney executive Peter Rice to take over as the company's chief content officer, ousting 10-year veteran Bela Bajaria. Netflix also dismissed Dan Lin, the company's head of film, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal changes. That came just days after it laid off roughly 1,000 employees including Lin's right hand Doug Belgrad as well as Sheroum Kim, the director of independent film, according to various media reports. It's unclear who Netflix will tap to take over Lin's position.The company aims to restore quality to the brand and utilize Rice's expertise in talent relations to lure big names in an increasingly competitive market.Still, Netflix executives seemed to downplay the change in leadership during the company's earnings call."Our business and our business flywheel are working," Sarandos told investors during the company's earnings call. "There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S. ... It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like."Sarandos said the streamer had "some really solid doubles and triples this year," but suggested the company needs more "home runs." Netflix's Ted Sarandos attends the 92nd Annual Academy Awards in Hollywood, California, Feb. 09, 2020.Jeff Kravitz | Getty ImagesIn an emblematic moment during Tuesday's call, Sarandos highlighted a deal with Disney, struck in October, to bring the Ice Age films and others to the streaming service, and gave a nod to that company's CEO, Josh D'Amaro."We already are seeing some of those benefits from the Ice Age movies. All five of them hit our top 10. That's really exciting," the Netflix co-CEO said. "And by the way, yes, Netflix just plugged a Disney movie on our earnings call. You're welcome, Josh." Netflix's content strategyIn a bid to capture consumer attention and broaden its subscriber funnel, Netflix has spent years diversifying its offerings to include video games, live sports and quick-turn documentaries on buzzy cultural moments. But more recently, it's lacked some of the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things," "Bridgerton" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriptions and viewership numbers.The cast of Netflix's "Stranger Things" Season 5.Courtesy: Netflix"We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," Netflix said in its shareholder letter Tuesday. "Engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy." And yet with Netflix stating plainly that it needs new avenues for growth — and against the backdrop of a foiled deal to buy the Warner Bros. film studio — investors and onlookers are once again looking at the theatrical business. "I think there's a place for the theatrical for Netflix," Matthew Condon, equity research analyst at Citizens, told CNBC. "Especially, as the competition for time and attention just continues to increase.""If they really want to build stickier fan bases around some of their [intellectual property], I think theatrical could be a good avenue for them to do that," Condon said. "That's one area that Netflix has historically not been all that strong in, is building like really, really strong IP. And I think building fan bases around theatrical releases and things of that nature can help with that and then also can help them get top tier talent."Netflix is no stranger to luring in big Hollywood directors. It's worked with the likes of Rian Johnson, Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuarón, Bong Joon Ho, Spike Lee and Guillermo del Toro. However, none of these directors' Netflix films received a wide theatrical release or a long run in theaters.Sarandos admitted earlier this month that the company has lost talent because it would not guarantee wide theatrical releases.Most notably, the creators and lead producer behind its hit "Stranger Things" have all jumped ship in the last year. Matt and Ross Duffer signed a four-year exclusive deal with Skydance — the new home of the same Warner Bros. film studio that Netflix nearly bought — while Shawn Levy joined the ranks of Disney to direct "Star Wars: Starfighter."Going to the moviesSarandos said Tuesday the company's strategy is about "specialty theatrical releasing," in which each film gets its own bespoke release. In some cases, Netflix plays the film in theaters for the minimum requirement to be eligible for awards. Others appear for weekend stints as one-off events, like in the case of its "KPop Demon Hunters" smash that ran in theaters for just two days.Gerwig's "Narnia" adaptation is among those chosen few to get longer theatrical runs and a wider reach, along with an animated film called "Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory.""Both films have big global IP and big global fandom, so we're very excited about how they'll play out next year," Sarandos said.Still from Netflix's "KPop Demon Hunters."NetflixIn another sign of its evolution into theaters, Netflix has said it will report box office results for films that have longer theatrical windows. Those readouts are standard for major studios, regardless of release or windowing, but the move marks a new level of disclosure for the streamer.Incoming content head Rice could be the missing piece for Netflix in a new theatrical model. The executive has a wealth of experience in television and film. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."But right now, Netflix doesn't have the infrastructure for a full theatrical commitment."Going into theatrical isn't quite as easy as I think sometimes folks make it sound," Steven Cahall, stock analyst at Wells Fargo, told CNBC. "You have to negotiate with movie theaters, and find spots for your films."Cahall noted that sending the occasional film to theaters, especially with a limited release, "maybe isn't so hard, but there is a muscle of theatrical distribution ... You need a team of people, and you need a pipeline of content that's intended for theatrical release, and you need a marketing department around it."That's where buying Warner Bros. Discovery's studio assets would have come in. In the absence of that acquisition, it's not clear how, or how quickly, Netflix can bulk up its own operations. Plus, it's previously balked at the marketing costs that come with bringing films to the cinema, which can total hundreds of millions of dollars per film. Despite a hefty content budget, Netflix has long prioritized quantity and seemingly endless choice for its subscribers over individual big-budget projects. A shift to a multi-pronged strategy that feeds both streaming and cinemas would require Netflix to more closely mimic the companies it disrupted in the first place. "So that becomes more of an existential question for Netflix: Is it time to become a media conglomerate rather than being a pure play streaming company?" Wells Fargo's Cahall said. "'Do we want to become a media conglomerate?'"

schema.headline: Netflix has dipped its toe into theatrical. Is it ready to jump in?

title: IBM beats on top and bottom lines as CEO Krishna touts 'Super Intelligence' traction
description: Arvind Krishna, chief executive officer of International Business Machines Corp. (IBM), speaks during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of
body: Arvind Krishna, chief executive officer of International Business Machines Corp. (IBM), speaks during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, June 22, 2026.Bonnie Cash | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesIBM shares slipped in extended trading on Wednesday after the technology vendor reported better-than-predicted third-quarter results. Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:Earnings: $2.95 adjusted vs. $2.86 expectedRevenue: $17.10 billion vs. $16.82 billion expectedIBM's revenue grew about 5% from a year ago, according to a statement. Net income, at $2.19 billion, or $2.30 per share, increased from $1.74 billion, or $1.84 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude acquisition-related adjustments. "Our clients are now deploying 'Super Intelligence' in ways that transform entire operating models, instead of simply addressing narrow or novel problems," IBM CEO Arvind Krishna was quoted as saying in a statement. With respect to guidance, IBM called for full-year free cash flow to increase by more than $1 billion. The forecast as of July was a bump of approximately $1 billion. IBM still sees 2026 constant-currency revenue growth between 4% and 5%.In the third quarter, IBM generated $7.80 billion in software revenue, growing 8% and topping the $7.66 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount.Read more CNBC tech newsMeta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reactionTesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declinesIntel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind scheduleInvestors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are risingConsulting revenue, at $5.34 billion, was flat and just below StreetAccount's $5.37 billion consensus."AI is increasingly embedded in broader transformations our clients are undertaking, representing about 30% of our consulting revenue in the quarter and 35% of our backlog," Jim Kavanaugh, IBM's finance chief, said on a conference call with analysts.The consulting unit's 27.4% gross margin narrowed from 28.9% in the second quarter. "We reinvested productivity gains into digital assets, accelerating our transition towards a services as software model to capture the growing AI opportunity," Kavanaugh said.Infrastructure revenue came to $3.70 billion. That was up 4% and higher than the $3.57 billion consensus from StreetAccount. The company's adjusted gross margin, at 58.5%, was narrower than the StreetAccount consensus of 59.1%.During the quarter, IBM said it agreed to buy Boeing and General Motors' HRL Laboratories, formerly known as Hughes Aircraft's research division, for an undisclosed sum.As of Wednesday's close, IBM stock has come down 15%, while the S&P 500 index has gained 13%. "I think the current street estimates for the year are about $32 billion of revenue," Kavanaugh said. "We feel comfortable with that $32 billion of revenue."WATCH: IBM CEO on quantum computing: Will see $1 trillion in value in by end of 2030swatch now

title: Tesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declines
description: watch nowTesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock slid mor
body: watch nowTesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock slid more than 3% in extended trading.Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:Earnings per share: 48 cents adjusted vs. 43 cents estimatedRevenue: $28.05 billion vs. $27.9 billion estimatedTesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up."I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger.Musk addressed the matter in his opening comments on the Tesla call, but didn't provide any additional information."I think I said everything that should be said yesterday," he said.Tesla's revenue was down slightly flat from a year earlier, when the company generated sales of $28.24 billion, according to the earnings deck. In Tesla's core automotive business, revenue declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion.Balancing out the declines were gains in Tesla's services and other revenue. Sales there climbed 33% from a year ago to $4.61 billion. Tesla blamed its lackluster automotive revenue and profits on lower average sales prices for its cars during the quarter, and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill a backlog of orders.Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a share, a year earlier, Tesla said. The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter.A Tesla Bot, also known as Optimus, is displayed beside Tesla logos at a promotional exhibition in a shopping mall on September 18, 2026, in Hong Kong, China. Cheng Xin | Getty ImagesTesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised), a partially automated driving system the company sells for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million."We believe that FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available, and we continue to work with regulators to get it approved in other markets," the company said in its investor deck.Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of Autopilot, said on the earnings call that the company plans to give some customer cars access to its forthcoming FSD (Unsupervised) systems around the second quarter of next year.Tesla is testing its Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but it's not yet sold to individuals. Musk said on the call that "the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transport-as-a-service." The company plans to bring Cybercab to cities beyond Austin, Texas, this year, Taneja said, paying attention to operating costs like maintenance, charging and cleaning. Musk said the company's driverless Robotaxi fleet will start to contribute to the company's financials in 2027. That fleet now includes 362 Model Y Robotaxi, and 449 Cybercab vehicles authorized for driverless operations in Texas, according to the state's Department of Motor Vehicles, "It's not like going to move the needle this quarter," Musk said, "I think it starts to become noticeable in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year."Barring regulatory intervention and protectionism, Musk predicted that Tesla "will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely."Tesla said its auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records during the quarter. However, the company has gotten meager growth out of its core market of late as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit.Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications.One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction.On Optimus, Musk said Tesla is "making good progress" on the AI systems that control the robots in development. He said there's "still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks." Musk said he expects current issues around electromechanical design, reliability, usage duration, and AI to be "solved around the end of next year."WATCH: Tesla and SpaceX form special committees watch now

title: Southeast Asia is hungry for AI — and the money isn't just in subscriptions
description: SINGAPORE - MAY 31: Scenes of daily life and the urban landscape are seen in Singapore on May 31, 2026. Located at the southern tip of the Malay Penin
body: SINGAPORE - MAY 31: Scenes of daily life and the urban landscape are seen in Singapore on May 31, 2026. Located at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, about 137 kilometers north of the Equator, Singapore is a city-state known for its modern urban environment and high standards of living. Green spaces integrated into the cityscape, multicultural communities and vibrant urban life are among the prominent features of the city. (Photo by Mustafa Hatipoglu/Anadolu via Getty Images)Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesSoutheast Asia is embracing artificial intelligence at a rapid pace. But the business of making money from AI is about more than getting consumers to pay for it.Generative AI adoption in the region has reached around 243 million people in less than three years, according to the annual e-Conomy SEA report released Wednesday by Google, Temasek and Bain & Company. That is equivalent to 58% of the working population, with adoption occurring four times faster than the uptake of mobile internet. Yet only 1% to 2% of the region's population pays for personal AI subscriptions, highlighting a gap between widespread adoption and direct consumer spending.Florian Hoppe, a partner at Bain & Company, told CNBC in an interview that businesses have found other ways to generate AI's commercial value from online shopping to digital advertising.Companies have been using AI to improve e-commerce conversion rates and handle routine customer inquiries, allowing employees to focus on other tasks, he added. Consumers may also be paying indirectly for AI when purchasing products developed using the technology.The findings come as Southeast Asia's digital economy is projected to grow 17% to $368 billion in gross merchandise value this year, with the market expected to exceed $1 trillion by 2035, according to the report.Hoppe also pointed to another factor driving the region's enthusiasm for AI: its willingness to embrace new technologies as consumers have shown what he described as "pragmatic optimism" toward AI, embracing the technology for its practical benefits. The region has historically ranked among the most active users of major digital platforms on a per-capita basis. "They're very experimental," Hoppe said, describing consumers' openness to new tools and services. He also added that in terms of individual markets, Singapore is among Southeast Asia's early leaders in AI adoption.That openness is extending to more autonomous uses of AI, with 75% of users willing to let AI agents find the best prices and complete purchases on their behalf. The report shows that confidence is also growing, with 62% of respondents saying they trust AI tools more than they did a year ago.Despite the rapid adoption, people in Southeast Asia still use AI far less than those in the U.S., with usage per person at just 10% of U.S. levels.For businesses, however, the potential returns are becoming more tangible. About 69% of shoppers use AI to compare complex purchases such as electronics, while early case studies show AI helping businesses boost conversion rates by 10% year on year and increase the average amount customers spend per order by as much as 75%.An example is Shopee, a Southeast Asian e-commerce platform, which now handles approximately 80% of customer queries through AI chatbots, helping cut its cost per customer contact by 30% year on year.In online media, Hoppe pointed to a "significant uplift" in advertising click-through rates and conversions through AI-powered advertising and improved targeting.But the benefits extend beyond online shopping. AI is helping travelers plan trips, making digital advertising more effective and enabling voice-assisted bookings for ride-hailing and food delivery services.Southeast Asia's online travel market is projected to grow 10% to $59 billion in gross merchandise value this year. Online media revenue, including digital advertising and streaming, is expected to rise 22% to $44 billion, while ride-hailing and food delivery are forecast to grow 15% to $40 billion in gross merchandise value, according to the report.

schema.headline: Southeast Asia is hungry for AI — and the money isn't just in subscriptions

title: SpaceX stock jumps 10% after earnings beat and Musk hints at Tesla tie-up
description: watch nowSpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a poten
body: watch nowSpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger. The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion. Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier. On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconSpaceX shares since its debut on the Nasdaq. Shares of other space stocks, including Rocket Lab, Intuitive Machines and AST SpaceMobile climbed on Wednesday.SpaceX forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, according to LSEG. "We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in the earnings release. Johnsen pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink, and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure. The company has dived into artificial intelligence this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. watch nowBull case for AI cloud providersCommentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note. "Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added.They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates."The shares of neoclouds Nebius and Coreweave traded marginally lower, while Iren and Applied Digital climbed in early trading on Wednesday.— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.Correction: Bret Johnsen is chief financial officer at SpaceX. An earlier version misspelled his name.Read more CNBC tech newsMeta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reactionTesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declinesIntel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind scheduleInvestors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising

title: Mortgage rates drop for the first time in 2 months, but demand still falls further
description: Homes in Daly City, California, US, on Tuesday, May 19, 2026. Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMortgage demand took another leg lower, despite a
body: Homes in Daly City, California, US, on Tuesday, May 19, 2026. Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMortgage demand took another leg lower, despite a brief respite from rising interest rates.Total mortgage application volume fell 5.3% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, dropped last week to 7.41% from 7.50%, with points falling to 0.75 from 0.83 including the origination fee for loans with a 20% down payment. "Mortgage rates decreased for the first time in over two months," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "However, lower rates were not enough to boost application activity, as both purchase and refinance applications continued to decline." Applications to refinance a home loan, which are most sensitive to weekly moves, fell just 2% week to week, a smaller drop than some previous weeks when rates were moving higher. Refinance demand was still 59% lower than the same week one year ago. With rates now over a full percentage point higher than they were a year ago, there is a very small pool of borrowers who can benefit from a refinance.Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home declined a steeper 7% for the week and were 18% lower from the year before. Buyers are reacting less to the weekly move in rates but more to the overall higher level. A report from the National Association of Realtors on Tuesday showed a sharp drop in September pending home sales. These are measured by signed contracts, so it showed the real-time impact of rising rates during the month. Rates remained at that higher level in October. Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.For those buyers in the market, a continued high share are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs, which offer lower rates but are considered riskier because they will eventually reset to whatever the market rate is at the end of their term. "The ARM share held steady at 10.5 percent, as ARM rates remained almost a full percentage point lower than the 30-year fixed rate, giving qualified borrowers a lower rate option to purchase a home," Kan added. Mortgage rates haven't done much to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. Last week was a particularly volatile week for rates, due to multiple monthly inflation reports. This week the moves have seemed to follow oil prices."But we'd caution against placing too much emphasis on the oil price correlation," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "It's been highly unreliable for more than a month." Correction: The National Association of Realtors on Tuesday reported September pending home sales. An earlier version misstated the day.

schema.headline: Mortgage rates drop for the first time in 2 months, but demand still falls further
